How does the hon. gentleman ascertain the amount of goods imported from England that have been partially made in Germany ? Mr. KEMP. I am making an estimate, which I think is a safe one. I believe that if there were no preference, we would import two-thirds of what we now bring in, which would be $17,270,481 as compared with $25,905,721. It is impossible for any one to calculate what the hon. gentleman asks, but I think that the estimate I have made is a safe one. I do not think there can be any doubt that our woollen people have suffered under the preferential tariff, and that some relief should have been given before this. The United States import about $14,000,000 worth of woollen goods annually. This Canada of ours imports about $10,000,000 annually. The American people therefore import to the extent of about twenty cents per capita while in Canada we import to the extent of $2 per capita, or ten times as much. There is no reason why these goods cannot be produced here, and it seems to me that if we are truly loyal to the British empire and to this country we will strengthen our own industries and in so doing strengthen the whole empire, for it can be no benefit to Great Britain that we should destroy an industry in this country when in so doing we do not appreciably affect any interest in Great Britain. But hon. gentlemen opposite want to know if we mean to do away with this tariff. Well, my policy would be to make every thing we possibly can in this country, to give to Great Britain a substantial preference over her competitors in such things as we do not produce, and allow no foreign goods whatever to come in under the preferential tariff. I do not believe that what the Minister of Interior told us last year meets with the approval of this country. He said : When we give a preference, if it is to be at any one's expense, it is at the expense of the manufacturer and workingmen of Canada. We go a little further, and say that it is the policy of the Liberal party of Canada to reduce the duties and to remove to some extent the burden of the excessive tariff which was imposed on imported goods by the late Conservative government. What have we gained by this preferential tariff ? We have gained the discrimination of Germany against us. We have thrown our workingmen out of employment to some extent. True, we have got the clauses in the German and Belgian treaties denounced, but up to the present of what advantage has that denunciation been to us ? It may be in the future, but so far it has been of no benefit to this country whatever. I would advocate a reciprocal preference in trade matters between the different parts of this empire on entirely broader lines than those which exist at present.	Let me draw attention to a press despatch * which appeared coming from London to the ' New York Post ' a day or two ago : So far as concerns the preferential tariff proposals now coming from Canada and Australia, , lesigned to make the empire more or less a ;rade unit, in view of the coronation conference in June, it is understood that the cabinet is inclined to agree to submit the whole question to a Royal Commissi in, upon which the colonies shall be represented. I wish to point out that the idea of a royal commission is one which unanimously gained the approval of the chambers of commerce that met in London in 1900, and the British government has been strongly pressed to appoint this commission. If the right hon. the Prime Minister can accomplish nothing further, when he attends the intercolonial council in Great Britain, I hope he will at least advocate the appointment of a royal commission, composed of home and colonial delegates, to consider this question of preferential trade. I think that we ought to join hands with Australia in trying to work out reciprocal trade giving preference to the products of the empire. I believe that in the future Britain's trade policy will be considered upon the true basis of expediency. I believe that she will have to do something, and what we want to do is to make ourselves more independent of other countries, as an empire, in trade matters. We should place ourselves in closer touch with the 400,000,000 people of this British empire. We should stand shoulder to shoulder in matters of trade as well as in matters of war, and make it our object to keep British capital and labour within the empire. In discussing this preferential tariff we always come to the question of the debt of gratitude which we owe Great Britain and how we should repay it, and hon. gentlemen opposite tell us that this preference was given Great Britain because of the support she has given us by her army and navy, and in every other respect. That brings ipe to the question of the colonial conference, and it seems to me that the attitude of the government in that respect is a very peculiar one. I have here a copy of the cablegram sent on the 23rd January to His Excellency the Governor General by the Colonial Secretary, in which the Colonial Secretary asked that certain questions be discussed at this colonial conference. The cablegram reads as follows : It is proposed by His Majesty's government to take advantage of the presence of the premiers at the coronation to discuss with them the questions of political relations between the mother country and the colonies, Imperial defence, commercial relations of the empire, and other matters of general interest. These are the questions which the Colonial secretary was desirous of having discussed. The Governor General's reply was : Referring to the several questions mentioned I in your despatch of 23rd January, the only one

which, in the opinion of my ministers gives promise of useful discussion ;s that of the commercial relations between the various sections of the empire.
The British 'people must have been greatly disappointed when they found that this government will not even discuss the question of defence. The government state very clearly that that is a question which they do not intend to discuss. I would like to ask the right hon. the First Minister how it is possible for him to consider the question of preferential trade within the empire or of getting a preference for our products in Great Britain, if he is not prepared to discuss the question of defence, and if he takes the position that Canada will do nothing for herself in that respect ? Not only " must the British people be disappointed, but our own people feel humiliated at this attitude of the government. We know that Cape Colony and Australia have been assisting in Imperial defence. I do not say that we should follow the example of any of these colonies. I do not say that we should tax our people for the purpose of the British navy. I do not say that we should bind ourselves to do whatever the British parliament might tell us to do. But I contend that we have come to that period in our history, as a nation, when we should be willing to assume some of the burdens which other nations have to assume with regard to their own defence. How can we, with the population which we have to-day, expect to escape the responsibilities which other nations liave to assume ? Do we expect to enjoy all the advantages of being a part of the British Empire and share none of the burdens ? Do we expect the British navy to continue to protect our shores while we simply do nothing to help ourselves ? I think this is a question which we should face in a manly way, which we should be willing to discuss openly in this House in order to come to some conclusion. This country is practically, in the matter of defence, in the same position as the most helpless, recently acquired colony of Great Britain. We are not doing anything in the direction of coast defence or of building up a navy of our own, and I submit that the figures I have shown with respect to the operation of the preferential tariff are not a sufficient return to Great Britain for the advantages she is giving us. We find Great Britain overwhelmed with responsibilities and taxation, and I believe that if we had been obliged to go through a similar experience to that which the people of South Africa have been undergoing, if this country had been attacked by a foe, Great Britain would have done as much for us, and more than she has done in South Africa. The time, I consider, has come, when we should consider our relations with respect to this question. We are a part of the British Empire, and the question to my. mind is this : Are we going to remain a Mr. KEMP.
part of the empire or to become absorbed by the United States ? There is no medium course. And I think that the consensus of opinion in this country is that we shall remain British. I believe that the people of this country from one end of it to the other, unanimously are in favour of British connection, so strongly in favour of it, that they will not listen to any other course. I do not wish to take up the time of this House in discussing this question at any great length at this time. But I think that the Premier should tell us, before he goes to this colonial conference, what his ideas are with respect to this question of defence. In looking up ' Hansard,' I find that the Prime Minister, in 1892, stated in this House :
I have again and again repeated that the goal of my aspirations is the independence of Canada, to see Canada an independent nation in due course of time.
I would be the last one to accuse the Prime Minister of harbouring any such sentiments at this day. I do not think that it is possible for any public man in Canada to hold such sentiments. But, in view of our peculiar trade relations and of the attitude of the United States with regard to us, in view of the fact that the question of defence has been suggested by the Colonial Secretary for discussion, we should have a pronouncement by the Prime Minister before he goes to London, upon the question of our political relations to the mother country, and upon that of defence. Yesterday I asked a question with regard to the contingents which had been sent to South Africa, with the object of finding out which contingent we had assumed the cost of transporting, arming and equipping and which we had not.	I will read the question and the
answer in order that the House may understand my object in referring to them now :

1.	Did the government arm, equip and transport by land and sea, at its own expense, the various contingents of troops which were despatched to the seat of war in South Africa, to assist in subduing the enemies of the King ?
2.	If not, what are the different conditions respecting arming, equipping and transporting the several contingents ?
3.	If the government did not, at its own expense, arm, equip and transport any one or more of the contingents, what was the reason for such action ?

1.	The government did arm, equip and transport, by land and sea at its own expense, the two contingents of troops which were despatched to the seat of war in South Africa, from Canada, in 1893 and 1900.	,
2.	The arming, equipping and transporting of all other corps were carried out at the expense of the Imperial authorities, as proposed by them.
3.	The reason is that the government deemed it in the public interest to act as they did, and if the hon. member is not satisfied with

that course, it is open to him to affirm by motion, the policy which, in his opinion, ought to have been adopted.
I am a comparatively new member of this House, and may not know as well as the right hon. gentleman the rules of debate. But, I knew it was open to me to proceed to take such a course as the Prime Minister pointed out. But, without having before me the particulars which he has given, it would have been a rash tiling for me to bring about a discussion of the subject in this House. Therefore, I asked the question in order to ascertain the facts so that I might judge what my course should be. My opinion is that it is quite clear that, in respect to this matter, we have done very little and that we should have done very much more.
I think it was a reflection upon our soldiers who were sent to South Africa to put them absolutely in the position of mercenaries. These men would never have gone to South Africa to flglit for any other flag except that under which we live. They went there to assist in protecting the flag and in subduing the enemies to the King. The government put them in the position of mercenaries, and that, I say is a reflection upon them which they did not deserve. I hope that when the cheque comes out paying the government for the transportation of these men from the inland parts of Canada to the seaboard and equipping them, that the cheque will be returned, and that we shall assume our fair share of responsibility. Consider what New Zealand has done. The little colony of New Zealand has sent to South Afriea more troops than we have sent. It is, proposed to send to Great Britain, with our premier when he goes, a body guard of nine hundred soldiers. When those soldiers go through the streets of London, it is not unlikely that the people will draw a comparison and say : The British government, of course, are not paying for these troops, but they are paying for the troops that the Canadians have sent to South Africa. It is unfortunate to find that we can send to London such a body guard of our soldiers-and I am glad that our representatives will have such a noble body guard, and that we should refuse to pay the petty amount, the paltry amount required for the last contingent sent to South Africa. What is the position of Australia ? It might be interesting to the House to hear the expression of the Prime Minister of Australia with regard to the relations between Australia and the empire. Speaking at a recent gathering at Melbourne, Premier Barton voiced the opinion of Australia on the subject of British unity. He said :
It was not true that this country would not remain a part of the British Empire, or would not be so loyal a part of it if it advanced in its democracy. The tendency of the British Empire was clearly toward the advancement of individual liberty. In taking up arms for the empire the states had acted with alacrity and
brilliance. Did it mean a subservient adherence to old forms and traditions inconsistent
! with British liberty V Not a bit of it. Did it mean that we were becoming an independent country not only in thought, but in action and would forget those from whom we sprang ? No. It meant neither a grovelling subserviency on the one hand nor an ill-considered, unthinking resort to a separate republicanism on the other. The truth was that the Australian character laid down its own lines of demarcation, and Britain's attitude to her colonies since the one great mistake at the end of the eighteenth century was to help them to realize their aspirations for freedom.
' Now, while I am prepared to say that we should not give away any of our liberties, and while I am as strong a believer as anyone in retaining the rights we have under the British North America Act, and while I would not leave it to the British parliament to say when and where and how we should serve, the time has come when we should consider to what extent we are going to help to defend ourselves and to defend our own commerce. We should take a strong, a manly stand, upon that question. Australia has a navy. She is now spending $20,000,000 upon new ships and $5,000,000 annually on maintenance. Cape Colony has done something along the same line, as well as Natal. The people of Great Britain spend no less a sum-not in war time, but before the South African war broke out-than $5.40 per capita on the army and navy. The people of the United States spend about the same amount, or about $5.50 per head. If we spent in proportion to the amount spent by Great Britain or the United States, we should have an expenditure of about $30,000,000 for defence. We actually spend about 40 cents or 50 cents per head. Every civilized nation in the world spends from $2 to $5 on arms and defence. On the basis of our export trade, as compared with Great Britain, if we spent at their rate, we should spend about $25,000,000 annually on defence. We need not go into any such extraordinary expenditure, and I am not giving these figures for the purpose of showing that we should. I do say, however, that we should to some extent start the nucleus of a fund for the purpose of building up a navy of our own, and taking such steps as may in some degree protect ourselves and protect our commerce, that we may occupy a more manly position within the empire than we do at the present time.
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to occupy the time of the House any longer; but before resuming my seat I would like to refer to one more matter. The Prime Minister said in Toronto that there was nothing to reform; he has also said that there were no burning questions in this country. Now, I would like to submit for the consideration of the government some burning questions which I think the government might well take into their consideration, with the view

of developing the country and acquitting themselves of their responsibilities. There is the question of the exodus; there is the question of defence; there is the question of purity in elections; there is the question of purchasing supplies and doing public works by tender; there is the question of strictest economy in the administration of the affairs of the country; there is the question of reduction in freight rates on farm and other products; there is the question of building up our foreign trade in the ratio of that of the United States; there is the question of improving our transportation facilities so that our produce may go out via Canadian instead of United States ports; there is the question of inducing Germany to stop discriminating against our farm products; there is the question of framing our trade policy so as to give more employment to our own people and thus keep them in this country; we require a definite and aggressive trade policy based upon the necessities of the country; and we should endeavour to frame such a policy within the British Empire, based upon reciprocal trade preferences which will bring us into closer touch with its 400,000,000 inhabitants, and render us more independent in trade matters than we are at the present time. We should also endeavour to settle the various questions in dispute between Canada and the United States. Sir, I submit these are matters that may be considered as burning questions, and I hope the government will consider them as such. It is not necessary for me to say that I shall support heartily the amendment submitted by the hon. leader of the opposition ; and I do not see why such an amendment as that should not commend itself to many hon. gentlemen on the opposite side of the House.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.

speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) :

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, while thus far I have not burdened the House at any considerable length, I, nevertheless, like the last speaker (Mr. Kemp), have some little hesitation after so much ground has been covered and so many very excellent speeches have been made in attempting for the first time to participate in a budget debate here. 1 believe it is the duty of all new members of this House for a time, at all events, to endeavour to watch the operations and business of the House, in order to attempt to get well acquainted with the duties that a representative of the people should be acquainted with in order to properly discharge the service which he should render to the country. During last session and this, there are two things which I have been attempting to do as weh as I was able.

One was to observe the conduct, the capacity and the operations of the members of the government behind which I sit in order to ascertain, how, in my humble judgment, they were discharging their duties which would be properly discharged by them, and another was to ascertain just what was the nature, the character of the criticism which leading members on the opposite side of the House evinced from time to time. If I were to judge from the criticisms I have heard from the other side of the House I would have commenced by this time to believe that this government was not the government that I had supposed it to be. I well recollect in 1896 that when the right hon. leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) was called upon to select a government, with what joy, with what satisfaction and confidence the Liberal party throughout the length and breadth of Canada, and also, I believe a great many of the independent Conservatives throughout the country, looked over the personnel of that government. They expected from their record, from their business capacity and ability, from their integrity and honesty that the government would take hold of the affairs of this country with a good grip, with an honest desire to serve the country and with a great deal of business capacity. After watching them for four or five years from outside this House and at long range, and during the past year from inside of this House at close range, the only opinion that I have been able to form In connection with the matter is, that toe government has answered the expectations that the Liberals of this country had in 1890 when it entered upon its career, and I believe, also, has lived up to the expectations that many Conservatives formed of that government at that time. On the other hand, if I were to express the opinion which I had formed from an observation of the criticisms of the leading members on the other side of the House during last session and this, it would be to the effect that they seem rather more to confine their attention to matters of small moment, to items of small detail, than to dealing with the large questions that the members of the'government deal with from time to time. For example, just within this session, on a certain evening, an item was up for consideration amounting to $5,000, and we were shortly engaged in a debate upon that item. The minister in charge gave his word, in view of the criticism of the item, that not one dollar of the $5,000 would be expended until he had an opportunity of looking into the matter and deciding whether it was an expenditure that should be made. While that was his representation to the House, hours were taken up after he had made that statement in a continuance of the debate upon the question of that particular item, although items of very large concern were passed without any comment at all.
Mr. Speaker, is this quite in order ?
I am afraid the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sutherland, Essex) is referring to a previous debate which is contrary to the rule.

Possibly I may be doing so in going into the details of that matter, but, as a matter of general comment, that has been the opinion I have formed from observing the criticisms of hon. gentlemen opposite during the past session and during this session. Now, while I have tried, as I think, to examine and follow the record of the government as carefully as possible, I have also sought in the best way I could to examine the amendment which the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) moved some few days ago. Although, gentlemen who have participated in this debate from this side of the House, almost without a single exception, have asked speakers on the other side of the House to come down to details, and to something definite in regard to what their leader meant and to what they meant, not one of them up to this time has ac-ceeded to that request. We are told in this amendment that the present tariff is unsatisfactory, but I do not know in what respect hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House consider it unsatisfactory. Not one of them has come down to details upon the matter at all. We are told also that the trade of the country needs for its development a policy of adequate protection, but what are the items of protection, what are the particular commodities upon which this duty is required, are unknown up to this moment. It does seem to me that the legal ingenuity and political sagacity of the hon. leader of the opposition have been used for the purpose of framing an amendment which is almost unintelligible and which would leave him all sorts of scope in the future, and in so far as its being a declared policy of a definite character is concerned, it is quite the reverse, and one which does not lay down any definite policy at all. It has been stated from time to time in this House and in the country that this is a country of wonderfully different classes; that we have a great agricultural class in one part of the country, a great mining industry in another part of the country, a great fishing industry in another part of the country and the needs of these industries and of the people from one end of the country to the other are diverse. It does seem to me that no policy can have any great force, or be of any great benefit to the country, that does not recognize that the first principle which should characterize that policy must be one of moderation, one of general application rather than one by which a particular interest, or a particular class, would be benefited to the disadvantage and detriment of
other great classes in the community. It Seems to me that if there is one thing that characterizes the policy of the present government more than another, it is that mark of moderation and regard for the interests of all classes. If I were asked what was the character of the industries of this country, I would naturally say that they are, agricultural, manufacturing, mining, lumbering and fishing. There is another great interest, that of the labouring classes, and I shall show in a few moments that this government has not been at all slow to recognize the duty it owes to the great labouring interests, and that from time to time it has done many things which are for the particular benefit and in the interests of that great class. If we look for a few moments over these various great industries to which I have adverted, we will ascertain the condition of our commerce as represented by the exports from this countfy in 1896 and again in 1901. If we look at the exports of animals and their produce we find that they amounted to $37,000,000 in 1896, while in 1901 they have increased to $50,000,000. If we look at agricultural products we find that in 1896 the exports were $17,000,000, and in 1901 $38,000,000. If we look at manufactures we find that in 1896 the exports were $10,000,000, and in 1901 $17,000,000. If we look to the exports in connection with the mining industry we find that in 1896 they were $8,000,000, and in 1901 $40,000,000. The only industry which, in a comparison between these two particular years, 1896 and 1901, does not show a marked increase, but rather a slight diminution, is the fishing industry, the exports of which in 1896 amounted to $11,000,000, and in 1901 to $10,000,000. But we all know that that industry is marked by great fluctuations. We know that, for example, in British Columbia for several years there has been great falling off in the catch of salmon, but we know also that the largest catch of salmon the country has ever seen will be that of the year we are in. What I want to try to make out is, that this policy is a general policy working for the interest and advantage of all classes as shown by the fact that each and every of the great Industries of the country during these past five or six years, has shown a steady, a gradual and a very large increase. So that, instead of this policy being one for one particular class, it is a policy in the interests of all classes. There is another point which is very akin to this. One would expect for five or six years, in order to ascertain whether this policy was a general policy, a moderate policy and one in the interest of all classes, that if you apply these tests which are ordinarily applied to ascertain whether a country is prospering or not, whether the policy that is in vogue has worked in the interest of the country; that if you apply these tests, some at all events of the tests

will show that the country was or was not prospering under that policy.
The first of these tests is as to a general and steady increase of trade. If we apply that test, then unquestionably the policy inaugurated in 1896 and continued to the present has been satisfactory and useful to the country. If we apply the second test: That of an increasing population, I do not think that any one that listened to the speech delivered by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) during this debate, can come to any other conclusion but that for the last five or six years while this government has been in power and while its policy has been in force, the depopulation of the country which was occurring during the Conservative regime has been gradually ceasing, and that a great change for the better has come over the country in that respect.
Again let us apply the test as to whether the value of lauds has been increased. I doubt if there is a single member of this House who has had any practical knowledge, who cannot say that in his vicinity the fact is patent that land values are steadily going up for the last five years, while prior to that they were practically at a standstill. Again, if we look at the savings of the people as evidenced by their deposits in the savings banks, has it not been- made apparent time and again that the people of Canada are rapidly becoming wealthy and are putting by far more of their earnings as savings, than they ever did before. Again, I have no doubt that many of the hon. gentlemen in this House can testify, as I can myself, that the liabilities which existed upon the property of the Canadian people are largely being reduced under the present condition of things. If I were to speak from my own knowledge I could name many cases in the county from which I came where farmers have during this year come in and paid off as much as $1,000 or $1,200 of the mortgage which was upon their lands for many years, that is evidence that the agricultural classes are now prosperous as never before and that the result of that prosperity is enabling them to wipe out the mortgage incumbrances which had been upon their lands for many years. Again, take the business failures of this country. Any one who studies the records of these failures in Canada for the past five years will see that the number of failures and the amounts involved in 1896, were far greater than they are at the present day. That tells in favour of this government as do all these other tests of prosperity which I have applied. Therefore, as 1 say, applying to this general moderate policy which the government inaugurated in 1896 and has persisted in, up to this day-with such slight changes as were rendered necessary from time to time-applying any or applying all of the tests which are ordinarily applied to show whether the policy of a government which Mr. SUTHERLAND (Essex).
has been in operation for a reasonable number of years, has been successful or not ; then undoubtedly the policy of this government has proven to be eminently successful. The hon. member for Grey (Mr. Sproule) in the course of his speech asked the question : What has this government done to promote the prosperity of this country ? I shall endeavour to tell him. There is one thing that the prosperity of a country depends upon as does the prosperity of an individual, and that is reputation and credit. These are qualities which stand as high and are as useful to a country in its operations, as they are to a private individual in his business. Reputation and credit are necessary to the private individual in the conduct of his business, and they are also necessary to a government which frames measures for the welfare of a country. We cannot perhaps answer this question, free from any partisan bias, but we may go across the sea and ask, what was the credit and what was the reputation of Canada when the Conservative government went out of power in 1896. We know that in 1896 that great newspaper, the London ' Times,' said
Here in the mother country, there is only a feeling of deep regret for the wrong done to the fair fame of the oldest of her daughters.
And the London ' Chronicle ' said in 1896 :-
It is no longer possible to doubt that corruption in its worst form is rampant in a large portion of the Canadian civil service.
Now, after six years, I ask hon. gentlemen opposite, can it be said with the slightest degree of truth that that is the reputation of the Liberal party, of this government, or of Canada in the year 1902. I have given you definite and positive evidence that outside of this country and among our kin across the water, that was the reputation which Canada unfortunately had in 1896.
I submit that if this government had done nothing more than to wipe out that stigma which rested upon the people of this country, they have done very much to secure our thanks, and they have done much also to promote our prosperity.
What has this government done for the country ? I think that the speech made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce served a very wise and very useful purpose in showing what this government has done for the good of Canada. In periods of prosperity like this, and when we are swimming along in a very happy and progressive way, we sometimes are prone to forget what were the conditions which existed in other days ; and when the Minister of Trade and Commerce pointed out, that prior to 1896 there was an era of deficits which has been replaced by an era of surpluses; that there was an era of stagnation in trade which has been replaced by a period of enterprising progress ; that there is more

work for the working men now than there was in those days ; that wages are higher now than they were then ; that the great agricultural industry and other business was at a low ebb then as compared with now ; I say that in pointing out those things and drawing a contrast between the conditions that exist now and the conditions that existed then, the Minister of Trade and Commerce served a very good purpose. Hut there is another thing which the people of a country are apt to forget and which it is well perhaps for public men to advert to from time to time. We are too apt to forget the services this government has rendered to, the country ; the practical legislation which it has introduced and the various other beneficial administrative acts which the government has performed during the past five or six years. With the permission of the House I shall for a moment call attention to these. In considering whether the government has served the people wisely and well, and whether it merits the criticism that has been levelled against it by its opponents, it is well that we should look to its record and see whether the ministers of the Crown have lived up to the ideal we had of them in 1896, as a cabinet of business men who would govern the country on business principles. Here are some of the things which this government has applied itself to, and which in my judgment it is entitled to a good deal of credit for. There was the settlement of the Manitoba school question ; There was the reform of the tariff and the reduction in taxation ; there was the preferential tariff introduced ; there w"as the development of transportation facilities; there was the abolition of Canadian quarantine on cattle exported to the United States ; there was the development of cold storage facilities ; there was the fostering of agricultural interests ; there was the adopting of a vigorous immigration policy ; there was the reduction in the postage rate ; there was the inauguration of increased postal facilities ; there was the reduction of the post office department deficit ; there was the government loan secured in the British market on most favourable terms ; there was the denunciation of the German and Belgian treaties ; there was the fact that Canadian government securities were listed in Great Britain ; there was the extension of the Intercolonial Railway to Montreal ; there was the development of the iron and steel industries in Canada ; there was the establishment of creameries in the Northwest Territories ; there was the establishment of the assay office in Vancouver ; there was the maintenance of the principle that government lands should be held for the settler alone ; there was the preparation of ' better trade statistics than we ever had before ; there was the principle of a fair wages to labour ; there was the establishment of the department of labour ; there was the publication of the ' Labour Gazette;'
there was the introduction of a form of conciliation for the settlement of labour disputes ; there was the abolition of the sweating system on government contracts ; there-was the development of the Yukon on the principle that the Yukon must pay for the Yukon ; there was the establishment of cold storage for the preservation of bait for the fishermen of the lower provinces ; there was the appointment of an officer to prevent the infraction of Alien Labour Laws ; there was the construction of the telegraph line to the Yukon ; there was the extension of the government telegraph line to the Straits of Belle Isle ; there was the attempt to prevent the discrimination of rates by railway companies ; there was the large purchases of food stuffs made by the British government in Canada. I submit that the recital of these various things done, works accomplished and legislation enacted by this government shows a record that has not been equalled by any previous government that Canada ever had.
I have sought in a few words to show that no policy can be effective in this country, whether in respect to trade or anything else, except a policy which is moderate and which js not confined to any one class, but is for all; and I am bound to say, in respect to another matter which the hon. gentleman who has just preceded me spoke of, the leader of this government and the government itself have made a record of which they may well feel proud. During the progress of this 'debate a great deal of attention has been directed to the United States and its people. There is no doubt that the United States is a country peculiarly favoured, having a splendid range of natural advantages and products, an immense population which has flowed to their shores, and another thing which we are often apt to forget, a great deal of British capital to assist in developing the resources of the country. AYe are sometimes told in this House' as well as elsewhere in the country that we have reason to fear an influx of capital from the United States. Did the people of the United States ever take that attitude towards the influx of British capital ? On the contrary, was it not gladly received in the United States, and was it not one of the most potent influences in the development of all the industries of that country ? And if at the present time we see signs of United States capital coming into Canada, and if in the future we are to see more, as I am satisfied we shall, we may say that in this respect at all events we desire the fullest reciprocity that we can have with the United States. Just as they gladly received British capital into-their country, we should gladly receive United States capital to assist in building up this country.
The people of the United States have afforded us an example in another respect. which we may well imitate. AVliatever their

mous quantity of contracts which they had secured. The owners of that concern, who within the last few years have come into this country and set up that establishment and already have it on a splendid business basis. Bishop Fur Company, which has been established as a new concern, an offshoot from an establishment at Wyandotte, Michigan. That concern has been established since 1896. There is another question I would like to speak about for a few minutes, and one which is attracting a great deal of attention, and that is the transportation question. One would think, at times, that this was a comparatively new question, and that the statesmen of this country were only now commencing to realize the importance of it. It is hardly that. Many years ago, this question was agitating the minds of statesmen both on this side of the line and on the other. For example I will read some words which might well have been used by the Prime Minister of this country to-day or the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Public Works instead of having been used years ago, as they were. In 1865, which, as you will remember, was the last year before the abrogation of the reciprocity with the United States, the Board of Trade of the city of Detroit, which is just opposite the city in which I live, called a great convention to discuss certain matters. The board of trade passed a resolution which they embodied in the letter calling delegates together. It was stated that the object for which the convention was called were commerce, finance and communications of transit from the west to the seaboard. And the president of the Detroit Board of Trade in welcoming the delegates to that convention used the following words in connection with the transportation question :

Communications of transit between the Great Lakes and the sea-board is of vital importance to the North-west. The continued prosperity of the great west demands additional outlets to the sea-board and to the markets of the. world for its agricultural, mineral and other products, which will crowd every outlet as fast as constituted.
Again he says :	.
Any measures which can be devised to ensure the west cheap and speedy transportation of its products to tide water will promote the immediate prosperity of the people east and west.
And again :
But. as the natural outlet of the Great Lakes the navigation

that is of the St. Lawrence.

is capable of being improved to give a safe
and clear depth of fourteen feet to tide water, which to the future of the great and growing west is imperative.	.
The president elected by these delegates used these words :
Gentlemen, when I stand here and look to the resources of the illimitable west, capable of sustaining one hundred millions of men here, and also capable of feeding another one hundred millions of men on the European continent, 1 ask you to multiply the facilities for placing this grain on the European markets at a price below what it can be grown there. Do your best; this mighty west will crowd these avenues to the sea-board to place this food in the eastern markets.	[DOT]
Such were the words of the men of that day. No doubt, these Americans were speaking, at that time, more particularly of their own great North-west. But times have changed, and we know that not only the trade of the North-west of the United States but the immense trade of the North-west of Canada is commencing to come down this great natural outlet to the sea. In my opinion, those who are taking this question up-and the government and the Minister of Public Works have been taking it up, and the hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Hag-gart) made an excellent speech on it last year as did also the present Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick)-should advocate every reasonable expenditure to make the outlet from the St. Lawrence and down to the ocean as speedy, as rapid and as cheap as possible. These men are doing a great work for the present and even a greater work for the future of this country. I agree also with something said by the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Johnston) the other night. Speaking of the deficit in connection with the Intercolonial Railway, and referring also to the administration of the cangl system, the hon. gentleman said in effect: We in the maritime provinces are willing that you should go on and administer the canals of Ontario, we are willing to go on with that expenditure believing it to be the complement of the Intercolonial Rail-

way and railway transportation to the sea.
I agree that that is the principle which must actuate us in this country, whether we ate from the west or from the east, whether we are from British Columbia, the North-west, Ontario, Quebec or the maritime provinces. We must be prepared to yield a little to one another, we must be prepared as the Finance Minister so aptly put it, to bear one anothers burdens in this country. It is in that way that the country will be able to prosper and progress as it has done in the last four or five years. A part of this transportation question is the railway rate question. I am glad to welcome the statement of the Minister of Railways that we are on the eve of having a railway commission in this country, or are seeking to have it. I do not imagine for a moment that a railway commission will cure all the ills of which we complain in connection with railway rates. It is not possible, in a country like this, for that to be accomplished. But, if a few men, wisely selected and having opportunities to study the matters, apply themselves care-/ fully and systematically to that question, there is no reason, as I see it why they should not gain information that would enable them to make much better practical arrangements than those existing at the present time. I am glad that the government appointed a man to go all over the country and get as accurate information as possible in this direction. In my section wo have a condition of affairs in relation to railway rates of which we think we have a right to complain, and I am glad the government are taking hold of the matter. We complain that Windsor and nil that district of Essex county is being discriminated against by some of the railways as compared with Detroit. One would naturally expect that if manufacturers or farmers wished to ship their products from the city of Windsor or from that section of the county of Essex, to the interior, they would be given a lower rate than on goods shipped from Detroit, for, it naturally costs something to transport merchandise across the Detroit river. Yet the fact was brought out by investigation held by this government officer, and also by the investigation held by the Windsor Board of Trade, that, in many directions the people of Windsor and locality have to pay a higher rate for the transportation of their commodities than do the people of Detroit or, for that matter people at points a good deal further in the interior of Michigan. A gentleman who is in a position to speak with authority on the fruit trade said :
The rate on a American fruit on a long haul is often less than for a short haul over a Canadian line, thus neutralizing the effect of the import duty. Peaches can be shipped from Grand Rapids, Michiganthat is about a couple of hundred miles, I think, from Detroit



to points east of Toronto at a lower

at an early date. Not only has this taken place the present year, but last year also, delegations came to Ottawa with the same object. Yet the hon. member for Essex (Mr. Sutherland) does not know what particular industry requires protection.

States, then I hope they will increase the duty; but it is entirely inconsistent for a gentleman who pretends to be a free trader and who supports what he calls a revenue tariff government, to make such a statement in this House.
